question: In agricultural practice, plant protection relies on stable access to tried-and-tested tools to control pests while minimising the use of chemical plant protection products. SILTAC is a product with active physical effects that has been used by farmers in various Member States for many years as an alternative to conventional chemicals.

Its availability has enabled professional users to plan crop protection in a predictable way, in line with the principles of sustainable farming. In January 2024, as part of the SCoPAFF Committee’s work, SILTAC was reclassified in the Commission’s working document entitled ‘Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 – scope and borderline issues’. It was placed into the category of plant protection products.

This reclassification took place without a transition period. In practice, it has brought about a risk that farmers in some Member States might suddenly lose access to SILTAC as a tool, without being able to replace it with equivalent solutions. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission looked into whether farmers have alternatives to SILTAC with a comparable profile and level of effectiveness?
What action does the Commission plan to take to prevent the loss of available tools to support plant protection in similar cases in the future?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.11.2026) The Commission refers the Honourable Member to its replies to questions E-000469/20261, the discussions held with Member States. The determination that SILTAC falls within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20094 results from the definition in Article 2(1)(a) of that Regulation.
The availability or effectiveness of alternative products to SILTAC has no bearing on the scope of that definition.

A comparative assessment of SILTAC with other plant protection products was therefore not required under the current legal framework, nor would it actually be possible, as data on the crops, harmful organisms to be controlled, conditions of use and efficacy are not available, given that the producer has not applied for approval of the active substance and for subsequent authorisation of a plant protection product containing it.

To address the consequences of the non-renewal and withdrawals of active substances and plant protection products, the Commission’s proposal for a Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package5 aims, among other things, to accelerate market access procedures for biopesticides, to clarify the scope of the essential-use derogation in Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 where no equally available, accessible and effective alternatives exist, and to enable Member States to grant longer grace periods for placing on the market and use of plant protection products following non-renewal of the approval of active substances contained therein.
